### 1.  What the game looks like  

* The hide‑outs are the vertices of the path  

\[
P_{20}=1-2-3-\dots -20 .

* On day \(t\) Bin Laden is at some vertex \(x_t\).

* Each day the U.S. chooses one vertex \(c_t\) to inspect.

undetected.

### 2.  A lower bound – Bin Laden can survive 19 days  

Consider the following “run‑away’’ strategy for Bin Laden.

* **Day 1.** Choose the right‑most hide‑out, \(x_1=20\).  
* **Night 1,2,…** Move one step to the left, i.e.  

\[
x_{t+1}=x_t-1\qquad (t\ge 1).

Thus on day \(t\) he is at hide‑out

x_t = 21-t .

Now look at any inspection schedule \((c_1,c_2,\dots )\) of the U.S.

\[
c_1,c_2,\dots ,c_{t-1}.

Let  

\[
R_{t-1}= \max\{c_1,\dots ,c_{t-1}\}
\]

be the rightmost hide‑out that has been checked so far (if none has
been checked, set \(R_{0}=0\)).  
Because Bin Laden moves left one step each night, on day \(t\) his
position satisfies  

\[
x_t = 21-t \ge R_{t-1}+1 .
\]

Indeed, after \(t-1\) nights he has moved left \(t-1\) steps, while the
U.S. can have inspected at most the first \(t-1\) hide‑outs on the
right‑hand side.  Consequently the hide‑out inspected on day \(t\) can
never be Bin Laden’s current hide‑out:

\[
c_t \le R_{t-1}+1 \le x_t .
\]

Equality would mean that the U.S. inspected exactly the hide‑out
\(x_t\); but this would require that the U.S. had already inspected all
hide‑outs to the right of \(x_t\), which is impossible because Bin Laden
has just moved one step farther left.  Hence  

\[
c_t\neq x_t\qquad\text{for every }t\le 19 .
\]

On day 20 Bin Laden would have to be at hide‑out \(x_{20}=1\); the U.S.
can now simply inspect hide‑out 1 and capture him.  Therefore **Bin Laden
can stay hidden for 19 whole days**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  An upper bound – the U.S. can always catch him by day 20  

We now show that no matter how Bin Laden moves, the U.S. can force a
capture on or before the 20‑th day.  The idea is to “sweep’’ the line
from the left‑hand side while keeping a one‑day “buffer’’ that the
robber cannot outrun.

Define the **search frontier** after day \(t\) as the interval  

\[
F_t=[\ell_t , r_t] ,
\]

where  

* \(\ell_t\) is the leftmost hide‑out that **might** still contain Bin Laden
  at the start of day \(t\);
* \(r_t\) is the rightmost such hide‑out.

Initially \(F_1=[1,20]\).

The U.S. follows the deterministic schedule  

\[
c_t = t\qquad (t=1,2,\dots ,20) .
\]

In words, on day \(t\) he inspects hide‑out \(t\) (the left‑most still
un‑inspected hide‑out).  We prove by induction that after the inspection
on day \(t\) (provided Bin Laden has not been caught) the frontier
shrinks to  

\[
F_{t+1}= [t+1,20] .
\]

*Base.*  For \(t=1\) we inspect hide‑out 1.  If Bin Laden is not there,
the only possible positions at the start of day 2 are the neighbours of
\(\{2,3,\dots ,20\}\), i.e. \(\{2,3,\dots ,20\}\).  Hence \(F_2=[2,20]\).

*Induction step.*  Assume after day \(t\) we have \(F_{t+1}=[t+1,20]\).
We inspect hide‑out \(t+1\).  If Bin Laden is not there, the only
positions that can be occupied at the start of the next day are the
neighbours of \(\{t+2,\dots ,20\}\); the left‑most neighbour is
\(t+2\).  Thus \(F_{t+2}=[t+2,20]\).

Consequently, after the inspection on day \(t\) the robber can be only
in the interval \([t+1,20]\).  Because he must move one step each night,
on the next day his leftmost possible position is exactly \(t+2\); the
U.S. inspects that hide‑out on day \(t+2\).  The invariant therefore
holds for all \(t\le 19\).

When \(t=20\) the frontier would be \([21,20]\), i.e. empty – the robber
has nowhere to be.  Hence the U.S. is guaranteed to have caught him on
or before day 20.  In particular, the robber can be hidden for **at most
19 full days**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Conclusion  

* Bin Laden can guarantee to stay hidden for 19 days (the “run‑away’’

* The U.S. can guarantee to capture him no later than the 20‑th day
